reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Presents with gradual painless blurring of vision, glare and haloes around lights, and reduced contrast, often worse in bright sunlight or oncoming headlights
Nuclear sclerotic cataract can cause a temporary myopic shift ('second sight') allowing reading without glasses before vision deteriorates
Posterior subcapsular cataract disproportionately impairs near vision and glare and is associated with steroid use and diabetes
The red reflex is reduced or shows dark opacities against the glow on ophthalmoscopy
Age is the commonest cause; other associations include diabetes, trauma, chronic steroid use, uveitis, and congenital or metabolic causes in children
Surgery (phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implant) is offered when the cataract limits daily function, not merely on its presence
In children a white pupil (leukocoria) demands urgent assessment to exclude congenital cataract and retinoblastoma
reference.pathophysiology: A cataract is any opacification of the normally transparent crystalline lens. With age, lens proteins (crystallins) undergo aggregation, oxidation, and cross-linking, while accumulation of pigment and changes in hydration reduce lens transparency and scatter incoming light. Depending on where these changes concentrate, opacity develops in the nucleus, cortex, or beneath the posterior capsule, each producing a distinct visual disturbance. Metabolic, traumatic, inflammatory, and toxic insults accelerate similar biochemical changes.
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination to grade and localise the opacity
Dilated fundus examination to exclude co-existing macular or retinal disease
Biometry (keratometry and axial length) for intraocular lens power calculation before surgery
redFlags: Leukocoria in an infant or child — exclude congenital cataract and retinoblastoma urgently
Sudden rather than gradual visual loss, suggesting an alternative diagnosis
A mature or hypermature (intumescent) lens that may precipitate secondary (phacomorphic or phacolytic) glaucoma
Associated pain or redness pointing to lens-induced inflammation
reference.prognosis: Cataract surgery is one of the most effective and successful operations, restoring good vision in the great majority provided the retina and optic nerve are healthy.
pitfalls: Attributing all of a patient's visual loss to cataract while missing co-existing macular degeneration or glaucoma
Delaying assessment of childhood leukocoria and missing retinoblastoma
Overlooking a myopic shift as an early sign of nuclear cataract
Recommending surgery on lens appearance alone rather than functional impairment
management: Phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implantation as the definitive treatment, offered when the cataract limits daily function
Interim optical correction with updated spectacles and improved lighting while surgery is deferred
Preoperative biometry with keratometry and axial length measurement to calculate intraocular lens power
Assessment and management of coexisting macular, retinal or optic nerve disease that may limit the visual outcome
Identification and control of underlying causes such as diabetes, chronic steroid use and uveitis
Postoperative topical antibiotic and anti-inflammatory drops, with monitoring for endophthalmitis and posterior capsule opacification
Referral to ophthalmology for surgical assessment
